flawed_step: Step 1, "every finite unit-distance graph in the plane has a proper 3-coloring", cannot be justified because it is false. The Moser spindle is a 7-vertex unit-distance graph that cannot be 3-colored.
counterexample: Moser spindle. Take a point A and two equilateral triangles ABC and BCD with side 1, so that D lies at distance sqrt3 from A. Take a second such rhombus AB'C'D', rotated about A until |DD'| = 1. This is possible because a chord of length 1 exists on the circle of radius sqrt3 around A. Suppose there is a proper 3-coloring. B and C are adjacent to each other and both are adjacent to A, so B, C and A use all three colors. D is adjacent to both B and C, so D must have A's color. By the same argument, D' also has A's color. But D and D' are at distance 1, so they are adjacent, which is a contradiction. The complete unit-distance graph on these 7 points contains every one of these edges, and any extra edges only add constraints. So it is not 3-colorable.
assessment_summary: The first clause says every unit-distance graph is 3-colorable. The Moser spindle, a 7-point unit-distance graph, refutes it: in any 3-coloring, both far tips would get the same color as the shared vertex, yet the tips are 1 apart. The definitions say refuting the first clause is enough, so the statement is false. The second clause is false too: the plane's chromatic number is at least 4.
